chunks: 'Abbad al-Basri met Ali ibn al-Husayn (blessings of God be upon him) on the road to Mecca and said to him: 'O Ali ibn al-Husayn! You have abandoned jihad and its hardship and turned toward the Hajj and its ease. Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, says:'

"Indeed God has purchased from the believers their souls and their wealth in exchange for Paradise; they fight in the way of God, so they kill and are killed — a promise binding upon Him in truth, in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran. And who is more fulfilling of his covenant than God? So rejoice in the transaction you have made with Him, and that is the great triumph." [9:111]
So Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Complete the verse.' And he said:

"The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the fasters, those who bow, those who prostrate, those who enjoin good and forbid evil, and those who preserve the limits of God — and give glad tidings to the believers." [9:112]
Then Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said: 'When we find those who possess these characteristics, then jihad alongside them is superior to the Hajj.'

key_terms.الجهاد: Jihad — in this context referring to armed fighting in defense of the faith, not inner spiritual struggle
key_terms.الحج: Hajj — the pilgrimage to Mecca, one of the five pillars of Islam
key_terms.الفوز العظيم: al-Fawz al-'Azim — the great triumph, referring to Paradise as the ultimate success
key_terms.سبيل الله: Sabil Allah — the way/path of God, the righteous cause for which fighting is permitted
key_terms.صفة: Sifa — characteristic, quality; the moral and spiritual attributes that qualify one for jihad

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Zayn al-Abidin say about the conditions for jihad being superior to Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narrative, Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin, AS) responds to the challenge of 'Abbad al-Basri, a Basran ascetic who questioned why the Imam was performing Hajj instead of engaging in armed jihad. The Imam's response — asking 'Abbad to recite the full verse — reveals that the Quranic injunction for fighting jihad is inseparably bound to the spiritual and moral qualifications of the mujahid. The Imam's conclusion establishes a conditional principle: armed jihad alongside those who truly embody the qualities of faith, worship, and enjoining good is indeed superior to Hajj, but such people are exceedingly rare. This hadith reflects the 4th Imam's context of living under Umayyad tyranny where armed jihad would have been misused; it subtly redirects focus from outward military action to inward spiritual rectitude.
